hook: A sunny park with no one in it: find each thing in the picture, then give it its article.
intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one sunny town park with 32 things to find in it, from the pond and its ducks to the playground — der Springbrunnen, die Wippe, das Eichhörnchen under the tree. The prompt asks Wo ist die Rutsche? and you tap it in the picture. A tap on empty grass or sky costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Rutsche?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. No object is asked twice in the same run.
tips[0].title: Compounds in the park: the last part decides
tips[0].text: Half the park is compounds, and the last word decides. Kinder + Wagen: der Wagen, so der Kinderwagen. Vogel + Haus: das Haus, so das Vogelhaus. Tischtennis + Platte: die Platte, so die Tischtennisplatte.
tips[0].check.why: The last part is die Decke, so the whole word is die Picknickdecke.
tips[1].title: Final -e usually means die
tips[1].text: Rutsche, Wippe, Hecke, Brücke, Laterne, Ente, Sonne: all end in -e and all are die. When a two-syllable noun ends in -e, die is the best first guess.
tips[1].check.why: Hecke ends in -e, and like most such nouns it is feminine.
tips[2].title: -chen makes every noun das
tips[2].text: The ending -chen always gives das, whatever the animal or thing: das Eichhörnchen. And watch the boat: das Ruder is the oar, das Ruderboot the boat — both neuter, but two different things to tap.
tips[2].check.why: Nouns ending in -chen are always neuter.
remember[0]: The last part of a compound sets the article: der Wagen → der Kinderwagen.
remember[1]: Nouns ending in -e are usually die: die Rutsche, die Wippe, die Hecke.
